article.text:
# dsh-superagent
> **Research prototype for reference only, not an official DeepSeek product.** This code grew out of our team's day-to-day development work, with much of the engineering done by coding agents. Treat it as research code, not production-ready software. It may still contain bugs, and its coding style and engineering practices may be inconsistent. Review and adapt it before using it in your own environment.
>
> We have adapted it for publication, so it is not identical to our internal version or the implementation described in *Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System*. Some designs discussed in the article are directions for future development and are not implemented in this prototype.
dsh-superagent is a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository, packaged as a bundle for [DeepSeek Harness](https://www.deepseek.com/en/harness/). It listens to GitHub and, optionally, Feishu. When someone allowed asks the agent for work, it opens a work item, works on it in its own agent session and directory, and answers in the original conversation, for example with a pull request. A web panel shows what needs a person.
It is also a way of working with an agent: **take as little human attention as possible, and give as much value as possible.** An agent that can act for a whole team can also waste a whole team's attention, so it acts only when asked or when a rule the team wrote allows it, and speaks only when someone must act or can use a result. [docs/000-philosophy.md](docs/000-philosophy.md) explains the principle and what it asks of the operator.
## Setup
Setup has many steps, so an agent does it with you. Ask your coding agent:
> Read SETUP.md in this repository and set up dsh-superagent with me.
It asks one short question at a time, shows the full plan once, and then installs and configures everything. [SETUP.md](SETUP.md) is what it follows.
## Documentation
Read the numbered documents in order; each builds only on the ones before it.
- [000 Philosophy](docs/000-philosophy.md)
- [001 Domain model](docs/001-domain.md)
- [002 Authorization](docs/002-authorization.md)
- [003 Execution](docs/003-execution.md)
- [004 Prompts](docs/004-prompts.md)
- [005 Panel](docs/005-panel.md)
- [006 Deployment](docs/006-deployment.md): manual setup, configuration, upgrades and troubleshooting
- [007 Architecture](docs/007-architecture.md)
- [008 Cookbook](docs/008-cookbook.md): adding a Source
## Development
`pnpm check` runs the typecheck, the tests and the build.

article.title: Prospero: a new coding harness for a more civilized age
article.text:
Prospero: a new coding harness for a more civilized age
October 31, 2026
nullprogram.com/blog/2026/10/31/
I’ve been fascinated with local LLMs for a couple of years now.
The better open weight models, including some that inference on regular,
higher-end consumer hardware at tolerable speeds, are now reliable enough
to handle simpler programming tasks. This requires a coding harness, but
so far this year I’ve been disappointed by all the harness offerings. For
inexplicable reasons most are built with web stacks, and consume enormous
amounts of memory. At its core a coding harness is essentially curl glued
to popen(). This should not require gigabytes of RAM. So I built my own:
Prospero. It’s written in my C++ style with a snappy Dear
ImGui docking interface. It uses around two orders of magnitude
fewer resources than other harnesses without sacrificing features.
Dark mode aficionados are covered, too:
Note that Prospero comes with no model providers built-in. You’re expected
to supply that yourself, such as with llama.cpp, a workplace on-prem
model, OpenRouter, Anthropic API, OpenAI API, etc. (You can’t use your
Claude subscription.)
For those unfamiliar with coding harnesses: In a chat interface you and
the AI take turns writing messages to each other. A coding harness extends
this concept, allowing an AI to “talk” to tools offered by the harness.
Tools “reply” with their outputs. A tool might read or write a file, or
run a shell command. An AI will go from tool call to tool call on its own,
looping on the results. Such an AI is called an agent. Occasionally the
AI will send you a message to inform you of progress or to ask a question,
and the chat interface is still there.
Some harnesses, including Prospero, allow agents to spawn subagents to
do their bidding, to work in parallel or keep their context clean. That
is, to not fill their working memory with subtasks. Agents can message one
another and coordinate on tasks. Given SSH access to another machine, or
over plain WSL, Prospero can deploy a headless copy of itself to other
hosts so that agents can operate on those systems. The Professional
Edition embeds engines for combinations of x86/x86-64 and ARM64 on
macOS, Windows, and Linux. The Windows x86 engine even works on Windows
XP, and can play solitaire and minesweeper if you ask.
The last is because Prospero is one of the few harnesses with desktop
control capabilities. If your model supports vision — any any model worth
using does — then it can “see” your desktop and interact with it. It can
click, type, and drag to test and debug GUI applications live without a
specialized, per-app MCP assist.
This headless engine is why no TUI is necessary. The harness engine runs
on the headless system, and the UI runs on your desktop or laptop. With a
little extra setup, the harness to run fully independently of the GUI, so
that it will continue without the GUI system attached — re-attachable
later.
Because Prospero is so lean, it may be the only harness that can drive a
fuzz campaign, particularly on a headless system, without the
Linux OOM killer targeting the memory-gobbling harness rather than the
out-of-control fuzz target that triggered it. So many times I’ve checked
back in on a fuzz campaign hours later, to find nothing was accomplished
because the harness process is gone.
(Why have an agent run a fuzz campaign? Because it can fix discovered bugs
on the fly and keep the campaign going! It’s a no brainer.)
Configuration
The configuration lives at ~/.config/prospero/prospero.ini. Easy to
edit. No JSON, thank goodness. Check it into source control, copy-paste
it. All the usual benefits. Alternatively, the Settings page can reach
every setting from the GUI, so you don’t have to edit the INI by hand. INI
files can also include each other, not just naming file system paths but
URLs:
include = https://example.com/prospero.ini
The idea is to allow a live shared or managed configuration. Includes by
URL are restricted in what they…

article.title: Jules Turndown | Jules
article.text:
Jules Turndown
October 29, 2026
We’re writing to let you know that as part of our work to unify our agentic coding efforts, Jules will wind down on December 31, 2026. You have until November 11, 2026 to continue finishing up sessions. After November 11, 2026, we will be turning Jules to read-only until the end of the year.
When we launched Jules, it was an experiment to learn how asynchronous coding agents could help you tackle your backlog and ship faster. What you built with it taught us where agentic development is headed, and those learnings are shaping products across Google, including our agent-first platform, Google Antigravity.
You can now export everything Jules knows about your work into a local folder: account settings, environment variables, scheduled tasks, connected repositories, memories, setup scripts, and every session, including its prompt, plan, full activity log, and code patches.
Your code, branches, and pull requests already live in GitHub, so they stay where they are. The export covers the configuration and history that live inside Jules.
To export, install Jules Tools and sign in:
Terminal window
npm install -g @google/jules
jules login
Then open a CLI coding agent, such as Claude Code, from your home directory and paste the export prompt below. The agent checks your setup, runs the export, and tells you what it saved.
Show the export prompt
Export prompt
I want to export all my data from Google Jules into a local folder: settings, environment
variables, scheduled tasks, connected repos, memories, setup scripts, and every session (prompt,
plan, full activity log, and code patches). Please do this in order:
1. Setup
- Check whether the Jules CLI is installed (`which jules`). If it isn't, install it with
`npm install -g @google/jules`. If npm isn't installed, tell me and stop.
- Check whether I'm logged in: `security find-generic-password -s jules-cli -a default`
on macOS (metadata only, without -w), or `secret-tool lookup service jules-cli username default`
on Linux. If there's no entry, ask me to run `! jules login` myself. It's an interactive
browser sign-in, so don't try to run it for me. Wait until I say it's done.
- Run `jules remote list --repo`. If it fails with a 401 and asks about GitHub, tell me to
connect my GitHub account at
https://github.com/apps/google-labs-jules/installations/select_target and wait for me to
confirm. If I've never used Jules with GitHub repos, I can skip this; the export will just
have no repo data.
2. Export: save the script below to a file and run it from my home directory. Then tell me what
was exported (the counts it prints) and the full path of the folder. Don't print my access
token or the values in env-variables.json.
Problems someone else already ran into:
- The Jules CLI stores its login in the macOS Keychain (service "jules-cli", account "default")
as "go-keyring-base64:<base64 JSON>". The script decodes that. The access token expires about
an hour after login; if you get 401s on every call, run any `jules` command or ask me to run
`! jules login` again.
- If ListSources returns 401 "missing required authentication credential" but the other calls
work, my GitHub account isn't connected to Jules (see step 1).
- Settings, env vars, repos and memories come from an internal `$rpc` endpoint. Sessions come
from REST endpoints under https://aida.googleapis.com/v1/swebot (/tasks, /tasks/{id},
/tasks/{id}/activities), which are what the CLI itself uses. Both are undocumented, so if a
call starts returning 404/400, tell me which one rather than guessing at fixes.
- The repo list doesn't include setup scripts or test commands; the script recovers them from
each session's code output (repoMetadata). Empty memories responses ({}) just mean there are
no memories.
- The API may return a few more sessions than `jules remote list --session` shows (older ones).
That's expected.

Today, we are launching the Plugin Marketplace in Antigravity, a centralized directory for discovering and installing third-party and Google-built plugins across the Antigravity App and the Antigravity CLI. Until now, connecting an agent to external systems meant manually configuring Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoints, environment variables, domain skills, and custom subagents across individual repositories or local configuration files. The Plugin Marketplace packages these primitives into verified, shareable bundles that you can browse by category and install in a click. Instead of switching between browser tabs to look up a ticket, inspect a design spec, query production logs, or check a security alert, you can give your agent direct, scoped access to the systems where your team already works.
As Antigravity continues to optimize for builders, we are launching the marketplace with…
